{{right|''Scott'', Guy Mannering, xi.}}}}

2. Thin or small beer. [Prov. Eng.]

{{smaller block|That too shall quickly follow, if
It can be rais'd from strong or ''tiff.''
{{right|''Brome'', Answer to his University Friend.}}}}

{{smaller block|Poor Mincing ''tift'' and ''tift'' all the Morning.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, ii. 4.}}
She ''tiff'd'' at Tim, she ran from Ralph.
{{right|''Landor'', New Style.}}}}

'''tiff'''<sup>3</sup> (tif), ''n.'' [< ''tiff''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] A petty quarrel or misunderstanding; a slight pet, or fit of peevishness.

{{smaller block|My lord and I have had another little—''tiff'', shall I call it? It came not up to a quarrel.
{{right|''Richardson'', Sir Charles Grandison, III. xxiv.}}}}

''Tiffania, Teffania, Thifania'', etc., a common fem. name), a reduction of ''theophany'' (ML. ''theophania, theofania'', etc.), equiv. to ''epiphany'', with ref. to the feast of Epiphany, the church festival also called ''Twelfth Day'', concluding the Christmas holidays. The name as applied to a silk would thus mean 'Epiphany silk,' i. e. holiday silk; cf. ''Easter bonnet'', i. e. spring bonnet; cf. also ''tawdry'', applied orig. to lace sold at a fair held on the festival of St. Audrey.] '''I.''' ''n.''; pl. ''tiffanies'' (-niz). '''1†.''' A kind of thin silk; gauze.

{{smaller block|The Knights appeared first, as consecrated persons, all in veils like to copes, of silver ''tiffiny'', gathered, and falling a large compass about them.
{{right|''Beaumont'', Mask of Inner Temple and Gray's Inn.}}}}

{{smaller block|Let her have velvets, ''tiffanies'', jewels, pearls.
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Noble Gentleman, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|A vestal veil on her head of ''tiffany'', striped with silver.
{{right|''Chapman'', Mask of Middle Temple and Lincoln's Inn.}}}}

{{smaller block|Doe we not descrie
Some goddesse in a cloud of ''tiffanie?''
{{right|''Herrick'', A Nuptiall Song.}}}}

'''2.''' A kind of gauze muslin, resembling silk gauze.

{{smaller block|How much shall I measure you of this ''tiffany'', Matty?
{{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, i. 6.}}}}

'''3.''' A portable flour-sieve made of tiffany. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''II.''' ''a.'' Made of tiffany, or thin silk: as, a ''tiffany'' cloak; hence, transparent.

{{smaller block|Enter four Cupids from each side of the boscage, attired in flame-coloured taffeta close to their body, like naked boys, with bows, arrows, and wings of gold, chaplets of flowers on their heads, hoodwinked with ''tiffiny'' scarfs. ''Beaumont'', Mask of Inner Temple and Gray's Inn.}}

{{smaller block|The wit that I took up in Paul's in a ''tiffany'' cloak without a hatband; now I have put him into a doublet of satin.
{{right|''Shirley'', Witty Fair One, ii. 1.}} ''Tiffany'' Natures are so easily impos'd upon.
{{right|''Mrs. Centlivre'', Beau's Duel, ii. 3.}}}}

'''tig'''<sup>1</sup> (tig), ''n.'' [A dial. var. of ''tick''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A light touch, such as is given in the game of tag or tig; a tap; a slight stroke.

{{smaller block|Andrew was compelled to submit, only muttering between his teeth, "Ower mony maisters—ower mony maisters, as the paddock said to the harrow, when every tooth gae her a ''tig''."
{{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, xxvii.}}}}

'''2.''' Same as ''tag''<sup>2</sup>.

{{smaller block|On the outskirts of the crowd, some of the town's children . . . profanely playing ''tigg''.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Education of an Engineer.}}}}

[Prov. Eng. or Scotch in both uses.]

'''tig'''<sup>2</sup> (tig), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A flat-bottomed drinking-cup, of capacious size and generally with four handles, formerly used for passing round the table at convivial entertainments. [Prov. Eng. or Scotch.]

'''Tiga''' (tī′gä), ''n.'' [NL. (Kaup, 1836).] A genus of Asiatic woodpeckers with only three toes on each foot, also called ''Chrysonotus'' and ''Chloropicoides''. {{smaller|The inner hind toe, or hallux, is absent (as in ''Picoides''). The genus is wide-ranging on the continent}} and many of the islands. The type is ''T. javanensis'' (formerly ''Picus tiga'' and usually ''T. tridactyla''), ranging from Java, etc., to the Malay peninsula and Bengal; ''T. shorei'' and ''T. everetti'' are the other species. The first-named is a handsome woodpecker, 10 inches long, with golden-greenish back, black tail, crimson occipital crest, pale-buffy sides of the head and neck striped with black, and the under parts rayed and barred with black on a light ground.
